datasets.name: Robomimic
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate state- and image-based tasks across proficient-human and mixed-proficiency demonstrations. datasets.name: CALVIN

Evaluate language-conditioned chains of up to five tasks; the common long-horizon protocol uses 1,000 unique chains, resets to a neutral robot position between chains, and advances only after task success. Report success by chain length and/or average completed chain length.

datasets.name: Meta-World

datasets.name: Franka Kitchen

datasets.name: LIBERO

datasets.name: Push-T

datasets.name: DROID

datasets.name: Open X-Embodiment (OXE)

datasets.name: FurnitureSim

datasets.name: RLBench

datasets.name: FurnitureBench one-leg real-robot evaluation

datasets.name: VLABench

metrics.name: Real-to-sim rank agreement (MMRV)

metrics.name: Pearson correlation between simulated and real performance
metrics.caveat: It measures linear consistency, can penalize rank-preserving nonlinear relationships, and can change sharply when real-world performances are close; report rank violations or another rank-sensitive measure alongside it.

metrics.name: Pose error (SE(3))
metrics.caveat: Separate translation and rotation discrepancies where possible; Euclidean or rotation-only errors can show only a limited view of pose deviation.

metrics.name: Object final-pose distribution distance
metrics.caveat: Averaging trajectories is invalid when objects have different final poses; compare final resting-pose distributions instead.

metrics.name: Validation loss
metrics.caveat: Lowest validation loss need not select the policy with highest manipulation success; compare with success of the selected, best, and final checkpoints where possible.

metrics.name: Success-rate-based continual-learning metrics (FWT, NBT, AUC, forgetting)

threats.name: Matched pretraining or initialization condition

threats.name: Matched task/order or data-sample rerun

threats.rules_out: Measures whether the result depends on a favorable task sequence or a fixed evaluation sample.

threats.name: Same controller with accurate versus estimated state
threats.detail: Run the same controller and plan using benchmark perception and a more accurate reference tracking system.
threats.rules_out: Separates controller or plan limitations from failures caused by state-estimation noise.
evidence: Benchmark for Bimanual Robotic Manipulation of Semi-Deformable Objects

threats.name: Performance relies on correlation between initial robot state and task rather than task inference
threats.detail: A policy can appear language-conditioned if task identity is predictable from the initial pose or context.
threats.ruled_out_by: Reset to a neutral robot position between sequences to break the correlation and test whether language is needed to select the next task.
evidence: CALVIN: A Benchmark for Language-Conditioned Policy Learning for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation Tasks

threats.name: A method's gain is actually due to action-space or control-setting differences
threats.detail: Policies evaluated with different action spaces or control settings can have different performance independent of the policy method.
threats.ruled_out_by: Measure the action-space effect with within-method ablations and, where possible, evaluate methods under matched action spaces; report any remaining mismatch.
evidence: Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion

threats.name: A diversity or generalization gain is merely a dataset-size gain
threats.detail: More training trajectories can improve performance even if diversity itself has no benefit.
threats.ruled_out_by: Compare equally sized co-training subsets that differ in scene diversity under the same mixing and evaluation setup.
evidence: DROID: A Large-Scale In-The-Wild Robot Manipulation Dataset

threats.name: Low held-out performance reflects poor optimization on training tasks, not generalization alone
threats.detail: A method that has not learned its training tasks well may also score poorly on held-out tasks, making the result ambiguous about generalization.
threats.ruled_out_by: Report meta-training and meta-test success separately; do not attribute low test success solely to generalization when training success is also low.
evidence: Meta-World: A Benchmark and Evaluation for Multi-Task and Meta Reinforcement Learning

threats.name: Planner ranking reflects a small or biased problem sample or a chosen parameter setting
threats.detail: Planner rankings can change with selected problem instances or sensitive parameters such as the range setting.
threats.ruled_out_by: Use a broad procedurally varied problem set, aggregate across all instances, and sweep the consequential planner parameter; report timeout and repeated-run protocol.
evidence: MotionBenchMaker: A Tool to Generate and Benchmark Motion Planning Datasets

threats.name: The policy exploits markers or the original lab environment rather than learning transferable manipulation
threats.detail: Performance may depend on recognizable markers, camera viewpoints, background, lighting, or other features unique to the original setup.
threats.ruled_out_by: Test with markers removed and replaced, and evaluate the same trained policy in independently built environments; report performance relative to the original environment.
evidence: FurnitureBench: Reproducible Real-World Benchmark for Long-Horizon Complex Manipulation

threats.name: A representation gain comes from its training data rather than its objective
threats.detail: A representation trained on broad human-video data may improve downstream performance even without the claimed training objective.
threats.ruled_out_by: Compare with a representation trained on the same frames and compute, then evaluate both with the same downstream policy protocol.
evidence: R3M: A Universal Visual Representation for Robot Manipulation

threats.name: A hierarchy gain is actually due to relative actions
threats.detail: Relative actions may simplify control independently of a proposed local-policy hierarchy.
threats.ruled_out_by: Compare the full method with a baseline using relative actions and with a condition removing the hierarchy while retaining the relevant action representation.
evidence: What Matters in Language Conditioned Robotic Imitation Learning Over Unstructured Data

threats.name: A headline gain reflects larger fine-tuning data rather than the claimed capability or limitation
threats.detail: Low performance may be due to too few examples, while a gain at a larger scale may simply reflect more training data.
threats.ruled_out_by: Measure performance across several fine-tuning data sizes and report whether the claimed effect persists across the scale sweep.
evidence: VLABench: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Language-Conditioned Robotics Manipulation with Long-Horizon Reasoning Tasks

threats.name: An apparent target success is a brief overshoot or pose-estimation noise
threats.detail: A target may be counted as reached even when the object only passes through the target region or the pose estimate is noisy.
threats.ruled_out_by: Require the target condition to persist for 10 consecutive frames and compare with the ordinary threshold-based count.
evidence: DeXtreme: Transfer of Agile In-hand Manipulation from Simulation to Reality

threats.name: Gains come from model size rather than the proposed mechanisms
threats.detail: A larger policy predictor could improve success independently of attention or dual-action mechanisms.
threats.ruled_out_by: Compare against ablations with the same number of policy-predictor parameters and measure the mechanism-specific performance difference.
evidence: Multi-task real-robot data with gaze attention for dual-arm fine manipulation

threats.name: Continual-learning results depend on task order or memory-buffer size
threats.detail: A favorable skill order or a larger stored-example budget can improve apparent retention independently of the proposed method.
threats.ruled_out_by: Evaluate multiple randomized task orders and compare methods with the same memory budget; measure performance across buffer sizes when memory is a plausible explanation.
evidence: Never-Ending Behavior-Cloning Agent for Robotic Manipulation

threats.name: Benchmark success comes from shortcuts rather than the claimed language or visual grounding
threats.detail: A vision-only policy may succeed through opportunistic grasping, while a language-only policy may exploit collisions or other task-specific shortcuts.
threats.ruled_out_by: Compare against modality ablations on tasks with stricter pose or grounding requirements and report task-level results, not only an aggregate score.
evidence: VLMbench: A Compositional Benchmark for Vision-And-Language Manipulation

threats.name: Poor task performance is caused by noisy perception rather than controller capability
threats.detail: A controller may fail with estimated poses even though it can execute the same plan with accurate state information.
threats.ruled_out_by: Run the same controller with accurate motion-capture state and compare against the computer-vision condition.
evidence: Benchmark for Bimanual Robotic Manipulation of Semi-Deformable Objects

threats.name: A simulator's real-to-sim relationship is an artifact of dynamics, visuals, physical properties, or simulator choice
threats.detail: Differences in control dynamics, rendering, object or robot properties, or physics engine can distort simulated success or policy rankings relative to reality.
threats.ruled_out_by: Pair real and simulated evaluations; measure trajectory tracking, test visual and physical parameter variations, and reproduce the evaluation in an alternative simulator.
evidence: Evaluating Real-World Robot Manipulation Policies in Simulation

threats.name: A performance drop is caused by ordinary image disturbance rather than a specific adversarial perturbation
threats.detail: Any image noise or patch could degrade manipulation, yielding the same apparent result as an optimized attack.
threats.ruled_out_by: Compare clean observations with random Gaussian noise and random noise patches under the same rollout protocol.
evidence: Diffusion Policy Attacker: Crafting Adversarial Attacks for Diffusion-based Policies

threats.name: Failures arise from task-allocation errors rather than action or object prediction
threats.detail: A multi-robot system may assign a subtask to the wrong robot even when its predicted primitive and object are correct.
threats.ruled_out_by: Supply ground-truth task allocation while retaining predicted primitives and objects, and measure the resulting performance change.
evidence: LEMMA: Learning Language-Conditioned Multi-Robot Manipulation

threats.name: A data-scaling gain is due to architecture rather than the added human data
threats.detail: When a method changes architecture as well as adding human demonstrations, the gain cannot be assigned to the added data alone.
threats.ruled_out_by: Compare the architecture with and without human data at matched robot-data amounts; explicitly retain the attribution limitation if the factors remain entangled.
evidence: EgoMimic: Scaling Imitation Learning via Egocentric Video

threats.name: A policy-comparison gain reflects an unfairly weak baseline or distribution-specific exploration
threats.detail: An alternative policy may fail because it cannot represent the demonstration distribution, or a structured exploration method may be unsuitable for tasks requiring off-manifold exploration.
threats.ruled_out_by: Verify alternatives can fit a deliberately simple multimodal demonstration distribution; test from-scratch exploration and report settings where the proposed method does not help.
evidence: Diffusion Policy Policy Optimization

threats.name: A reported aggregate-score gain is sampling variation or fixed-benchmark overfitting
threats.detail: Top-line averages can hide paired task- and sample-level variation, and fixed evaluation poses or manifests can reward memorization.
threats.ruled_out_by: Use paired task-level outcomes and a task-stratified test where available; redraw evaluation samples or poses from the same generator with matched local calibrations, and classify aggregate-only comparisons as inconclusive when bounds do not resolve them.
evidence: What Are We Actually Benchmarking in Robot Manipulation?

threats.name: A high simulated score reflects proximity of training data to the test setup rather than general capability
threats.detail: A policy may perform well because its training demonstrations were collected near the simulated test environment.
threats.ruled_out_by: Compare with a separately trained policy using demonstrations collected near the test and report the matched task results, making training-source proximity explicit.
evidence: What Are We Actually Benchmarking in Robot Manipulation?

evidence_standards.name: Inference setting
evidence_standards.detail: For real-world experiments, DDIM uses 100 training iterations and 10 inference iterations; the paper reports 0.1-second inference latency on an Nvidia 3080 GPU.

datasets.name: DROID
datasets.eval_protocol: Used to train policies and for dataset-diversity analysis. Policy training mixes batches 50/50 with the task-specific in-domain data and excludes episodes marked unsuccessful. For diversity analysis, one randomly sampled third-person camera frame per episode and the provided language instructions are used; verbs and objects are extracted with a semantic parser, and verbs are deduplicated with GPT-4.

datasets.name: Open X-Embodiment (OXE)
datasets.eval_protocol: Used for 50/50 co-training with task-specific in-domain data. The paper uses a curated split based on Octo Model Team et al., removing Language Table (5% of the Octo training mix). Policies are evaluated on the same task settings as the other approaches.

datasets.name: BridgeData V2 (Bridge V2)
datasets.eval_protocol: Included in dataset-diversity analysis using one randomly sampled third-person camera frame per episode and the provided language instructions; verb and object analysis uses semantic parsing, with verbs deduplicated using GPT-4.

datasets.name: RT-1
datasets.eval_protocol: Included in dataset-diversity analysis using one randomly sampled third-person camera frame per episode and the provided language instructions; verb and object analysis uses semantic parsing, with verbs deduplicated using GPT-4.

datasets.name: RH20T
datasets.eval_protocol: Included in dataset-diversity analysis using one randomly sampled third-person camera frame per episode and the provided language instructions; verb and object analysis uses semantic parsing, with verbs deduplicated using GPT-4.

baselines.name: No Co-training
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the same diffusion-policy backbone and task-specific in-domain demonstrations as the DROID condition, but trains without co-training data; evaluated on the same task settings.

baselines.name: OXE
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the same diffusion-policy backbone and task-specific in-domain data as the DROID condition, with batches mixed 50/50 with the curated OXE split; evaluated on the same task settings.

controls.name: No Co-training
controls.detail: The task policy trained only on in-domain demonstrations, without DROID co-training.
controls.rules_out: That the result is explained by the task-specific demonstrations and policy pipeline alone; a difference supports a benefit from adding DROID co-training.

controls.name: DROID (7k, 20 Scenes)
controls.detail: Uses 7,362 successful DROID trajectories selected from the 20 scenes with the most demonstrations, compared with a uniform random sample of 7,362 successful trajectories from diverse scenes; both use the same 50/50 co-training paradigm with task data.
controls.rules_out: That the diverse-scene subset's OOD advantage is simply due to using more DROID trajectories.

confounds.name: The benefit of diverse DROID scenes could be due merely to dataset size
confounds.detail: The stronger OOD performance of co-training with diverse DROID scenes might occur even if scene diversity itself were not beneficial, simply because more DROID data was used.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare a 7,362-trajectory subset from 20 scenes with a uniform random 7,362-trajectory subset retaining scene diversity, using the same co-training setup, and evaluate on the OOD task settings.

evidence_standards.name: 10 rollouts per task setting and method; success rate averaged across tasks with standard error
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports A/B evaluations using 10 rollouts for each task setting and method, and presents success rates averaged across tasks with standard error; it does not specify a statistical test or a threshold for calling differences real.

datasets.name: Meta-World ML1
datasets.eval_protocol: Meta-train on 50 random object/goal positions and meta-test on 50 held-out positions for reach, push, and pick-and-place; goal positions are omitted from observations. Score with task-specific success criteria (typically object-goal distance below a threshold; 5 cm is an example). Results use 10 seeds; adaptation episode count is not specified.

datasets.name: Meta-World MT10
datasets.eval_protocol: Train one multi-task policy across 10 task environments (500 training tasks total), with fixed object and goal positions and a one-hot task ID. Report average training success using task-specific success criteria. Results use 10 seeds.

datasets.name: Meta-World MT50
datasets.eval_protocol: Train one multi-task policy across all 50 task environments (2,500 training tasks total), with fixed object and goal positions and a one-hot task ID. Report average training success using task-specific success criteria. Results use 10 seeds.

datasets.name: Meta-World ML10
datasets.eval_protocol: Meta-train on 10 tasks and hold out 5 tasks for meta-testing; object and goal positions are randomized, task IDs are not provided, and training tasks are selected for structural similarity to test tasks. Report meta-train and meta-test success using task-specific success criteria. Results use 10 seeds; adaptation episode count is not specified.

datasets.name: Meta-World ML45
datasets.eval_protocol: Meta-train on 45 tasks and hold out 5 tasks for meta-testing; object and goal positions are randomized, task IDs are not provided, and training tasks are selected for structural similarity to test tasks. Report meta-train and meta-test success using task-specific success criteria. Results use 10 seeds; adaptation episode count is not specified.

metrics.name: Task success rate
metrics.caveat: The paper says reward values are not directly indicative of policy success; it instead evaluates with interpretable, task-specific success criteria, typically based on object-goal distance (5 cm is an example threshold).

confounds.name: Weak meta-test performance may reflect difficulty optimizing the meta-training tasks, rather than only poor generalization
confounds.detail: The paper notes that meta-training performance is also considerably below perfect, so low test success could arise alongside optimization problems on training tasks.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports meta-train and meta-test success separately, but does not rule out this explanation; it notes the meta-training results leave room for improvement.

confounds.name: PEARL's weak performance may be due to difficulty training its task encoder
confounds.detail: The paper explicitly suggests this as a possible explanation for PEARL's weak result, rather than evidence solely about the benchmark or method's generalization ability.
confounds.ruled_out_by: No measurement to test or rule out this explanation is reported.

evidence_standards.name: 10 seeds; average maximum success rate
evidence_standards.detail: Results are reported on 10 seeds, and Table 1 gives average maximum success rates over tasks. The paper does not specify confidence intervals, another variance summary, or a statistical significance test.

datasets.name: UR5 shelf-picking dataset
datasets.eval_protocol: 100 feasible motion-planning problems; each problem solved 20 times with a 60-second timeout. Planner timing is compared across the problems; two adversarial orderings of the same problems illustrate how conclusions can change when only a subset is used.

datasets.name: Panda box-picking dataset
datasets.eval_protocol: 100 motion-planning problems; each planner run 5 times per problem with a 180-second planning time. Reports the median best normalized cost and a 99% confidence interval across runs; cost is joint path length.

datasets.name: MotionBenchMaker prefabricated datasets (12 evaluated datasets)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates 12 datasets across geometric and sensed (octomap) representations, using 3 robots (Fetch, UR5, Baxter) and 4 environments. Each dataset has 100 problems. Sweeps the planners’ range parameter from 0 to 7 in increments of 0.25; reports average planning time over the 100 problems on a log scale, with a 60-second timeout.

baselines.name: BiEST
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same 100 UR5 shelf problems as RRTConnect, with 20 runs per problem and a 60-second timeout. In the prefab-dataset evaluation, compared with BKPIECE and RRTConnect over the same problems and range-parameter sweep.

baselines.name: RRTConnect
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same 100 UR5 shelf problems as BiEST, with 20 runs per problem and a 60-second timeout; tested with range values 0.05 and 0.5. In the prefab-dataset evaluation, compared with BKPIECE and BiEST over the same problems and range-parameter sweep.

baselines.name: RRT*
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with BIT* and AIT* on the same Panda box-picking problems, with 5 runs per problem and 180 seconds of planning time.

baselines.name: BIT*
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with RRT* and AIT* on the same Panda box-picking problems, with 5 runs per problem and 180 seconds of planning time.

baselines.name: AIT*
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with RRT* and BIT* on the same Panda box-picking problems, with 5 runs per problem and 180 seconds of planning time.

baselines.name: BKPIECE
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with BiEST and RRTConnect on the same prefabricated-dataset problems, with the range parameter swept from 0 to 7 in increments of 0.25 and a 60-second timeout.

metrics.name: Planning time
metrics.caveat: Results from only a few problem instances can give the wrong planner ranking; the paper reports results over 100 problems and shows that adversarial orderings of those problems can change conclusions based on small subsets.

metrics.name: Best normalized cost
metrics.caveat: Results on a single problem instance can suggest a different best planner than results aggregated across problems; the paper reports the median across all 100 problems and a 99% confidence interval. Cost is joint path length.

confounds.name: Planner ranking is an artifact of selecting a small or biased set of problem instances
confounds.detail: A planner can appear faster or better on a small set even when the ranking changes across the full task distribution.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Uses 100 procedurally varied problems and demonstrates how two adversarial orderings of the same problems yield different conclusions for small subsets; reports aggregate results across all 100.

confounds.name: Apparent planner performance depends on the chosen range parameter
confounds.detail: Range controls the rate of configuration-space expansion and can substantially affect planning performance, so a ranking at one setting may not represent the planners’ performance across settings.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Sweeps the range parameter from 0 to 7 in increments of 0.25 for the planners in the prefabricated-dataset evaluation and reports performance across the sweep.

evidence_standards.name: Repeated planning runs for timing comparisons
evidence_standards.detail: Each UR5 shelf problem is solved 20 times with a 60-second timeout; the prefab-dataset timing results report average planning time over 100 problems, also with a 60-second timeout.

evidence_standards.name: Repeated runs and confidence intervals for cost comparisons
evidence_standards.detail: Each Panda box problem is run 5 times with a 180-second planning time; the paper reports the median best normalized cost and a 99% confidence interval.

datasets.name: FurnitureBench
datasets.eval_protocol: Real-robot evaluation covers the furniture tasks and initialization levels described in the paper. Full-assembly policies are evaluated for 10 episodes with initial configurations set using the provided initialization guide; trials stop on task completion, 5 seconds without motion, unsafe movement, more than 350 steps per skill, or more than 3000 total steps. The single-skill benchmark evaluates the first five skills of each furniture model on low and medium initialization levels, with 10 trials per skill. The one_leg analysis evaluates low and medium initialization levels. Reported scores include success rate and completed phases. RGB inputs use a front-view image downsampled from 1280×720 to 455×256 and center-cropped to 224×224, and a wrist image downsampled to 224×224.

datasets.name: FurnitureSim
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates one_leg assembly under low initialization randomness, varying demonstration-data size and algorithm/visual-encoder configuration; reports success rate and average completed phases. The paper does not specify an episode count for these simulation evaluations.

baselines.name: BC (Behavioral Cloning; BC-ResNet18 in the real-world experiments)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with IQL on the benchmark tasks and demonstration-data settings; policies are evaluated under the same task initialization and scoring procedure. The paper does not specify a common hyperparameter-tuning or statistical-comparison procedure.

baselines.name: IQL (Implicit Q-Learning; IQL-R3M in the real-world experiments)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with BC on the benchmark tasks and demonstration-data settings; policies are evaluated under the same task initialization and scoring procedure. The paper does not specify a common hyperparameter-tuning or statistical-comparison procedure.

metrics.name: Success rate
metrics.caveat: A binary task-success score does not show partial progress; the paper also reports the number of completed phases.

metrics.name: Number of completed phases
metrics.caveat: It is a measure of progress rather than full task success; the paper reports success rate alongside it, and the maximum phase count represents task success.

metrics.name: Number of completed part assemblies
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that this measure is mostly zero with the tested algorithms, so it reports completed phases as a finer-grained measure of progress.

controls.name: Front camera only
controls.detail: Train and evaluate a policy using only the front-view camera instead of the front-view and wrist-camera inputs.
controls.rules_out: A difference from the usual two-camera condition supports the contribution of wrist-camera observations to performance.

controls.name: No AprilTag
controls.detail: Evaluate the IQL-R3M policy after removing the AprilTags from the furniture models.
controls.rules_out: Performance that remains without AprilTags argues against the policy relying on the original markers.

controls.name: Random AprilTag
controls.detail: Evaluate the IQL-R3M policy after replacing the original markers with different, random AprilTags.
controls.rules_out: Performance that remains with different markers argues against exploiting the particular original AprilTag information.

confounds.name: The policy exploits AprilTag markers rather than learning manipulation
confounds.detail: The apparent performance could depend on recognizing or exploiting the original AprilTags, rather than on the claimed vision-based manipulation capability.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate IQL-R3M with the markers removed and with different random markers; performance remains reasonable in both conditions.

confounds.name: Benchmark performance depends on the original lab environment
confounds.detail: Results might reflect the original environment's particular camera viewpoints, background, or lighting rather than being reproducible in independently built environments.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Have 10 participants build new environments and evaluate the same fully trained IQL-R3M policy on one_leg under low randomness; the new environments achieve 75–93% of the original environment's performance.

evidence_standards.name: 10 evaluation trials/episodes; report averages and min–max ranges
evidence_standards.detail: Single-skill success rates are averaged over 10 trials; the paper states that policy evaluation uses 10 episodes and reports average completed phases, with min–max error bars in the full-assembly results. No statistical test or significance threshold is specified.

evidence_standards.name: 10 independently built environments for the reproducibility test
evidence_standards.detail: Ten participants each build an environment; the paper reports average performance and states the new environments reach 75–93% of the original environment's performance.

datasets.name: LIBERO-Spatial
datasets.eval_protocol: 10 sequential tasks; evaluated using success-rate-based FWT, NBT, and AUC. Evaluation episodes or trials per task are not specified.

datasets.name: LIBERO-Object
datasets.eval_protocol: 10 sequential tasks; evaluated using success-rate-based FWT, NBT, and AUC. Evaluation episodes or trials per task are not specified.

datasets.name: LIBERO-Goal
datasets.eval_protocol: 10 sequential tasks; evaluated using success-rate-based FWT, NBT, and AUC. Evaluation episodes or trials per task are not specified.

datasets.name: LIBERO-Long
datasets.eval_protocol: 10 long-horizon tasks from LIBERO-100, used for downstream lifelong-learning evaluation; evaluated using success-rate-based FWT, NBT, and AUC. Evaluation episodes or trials per task are not specified.

baselines.name: SeqL (sequential finetuning)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with ER, EWC, PackNet, and MTL using the same ResNet-T policy architecture on each task suite.

baselines.name: Experience Replay (ER)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with SeqL, EWC, PackNet, and MTL using the same ResNet-T policy architecture on each task suite; also used with ResNet-T in the language-embedding comparison.

baselines.name: Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with SeqL, ER, PackNet, and MTL using the same ResNet-T policy architecture on each task suite.

baselines.name: PackNet
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with SeqL, ER, EWC, and MTL using the same ResNet-T policy architecture on each task suite; architecture comparisons also report results using PackNet across the policy architectures.

baselines.name: Multitask learning (MTL)
baselines.fair_comparison: Included as a reference alongside the lifelong-learning algorithms using the same ResNet-T policy architecture on each task suite.

baselines.name: CLIP embeddings
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with BERT, GPT-2, and Task-ID embeddings using ResNet-T and ER on LIBERO-Long.

baselines.name: GPT-2 embeddings
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with BERT, CLIP, and Task-ID embeddings using ResNet-T and ER on LIBERO-Long.

baselines.name: Task-ID embeddings
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with BERT, CLIP, and GPT-2 embeddings using ResNet-T and ER on LIBERO-Long; generated by encoding “Task + ID” with pretrained BERT.

metrics.name: Success rate
metrics.caveat: The paper says success rate is more reliable for manipulation policies than training loss, and uses success rate rather than training loss to compute the reported lifelong-learning metrics.

controls.name: Training from scratch (no pretraining)
controls.detail: Compared with models pretrained by behavioral cloning on LIBERO-90 before downstream learning on LIBERO-Long.
controls.rules_out: A downstream result attributable merely to having performed pretraining; the comparison tests whether pretraining changes downstream performance.

controls.name: Task-ID embedding
controls.detail: Uses a BERT embedding of a string such as “Task 5” instead of the natural-language task description; compared with pretrained BERT, CLIP, and GPT-2 embeddings under the same ResNet-T and ER setup.
controls.rules_out: That any observed difference is due simply to supplying a task-identifying embedding rather than semantic information in the task description.

evidence_standards.name: Three random seeds; report mean and standard error
evidence_standards.detail: Used for the reported performance tables.

evidence_standards.name: Two-tailed Student’s t-test with equal sample sizes and unequal variance; p-value 0.05
evidence_standards.detail: Used to mark statistically significant improvements in Tables 1 and 2.

evidence_standards.name: Five task orderings; error bars show standard deviation for a fixed ordering
evidence_standards.detail: Used in the task-ordering study; the paper reports a statistically significant ordering-related difference for PackNet.

datasets.name: Rubik’s Cube manipulation benchmark (Rubiks-M-N)
datasets.eval_protocol: On a PR2, attempt the specified tiers: M consecutive trials, each requiring pickup and N rotations on a distinct prescribed sequence. Sequences are generated by the provided software with a fixed seed. The cube starts on a flat surface at the specified position and orientation; the final state is validated with the provided software. A correct trial is scored by elapsed time from first contact to termination; tier scores are average time and standard deviation. The paper reports completed tiers and their scores.

baselines.name: Dead reckoning baseline
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with the fingertip sensor aided baseline on the PR2 using the same finite-state-machine approach for mapping rotation sequences to robot poses; this baseline uses an initial camera estimate and then no further sensor feedback.

baselines.name: Fingertip sensor aided baseline
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with dead reckoning on the PR2 using the same finite-state-machine approach; this baseline re-estimates cube pose with optical time-of-flight sensors before re-grasps.

metrics.name: Tier completion / manipulation accuracy
metrics.caveat: The benchmark reports overall sequence completion, not statistics on individual manipulation actions; the authors omit per-action statistics for practicality.

metrics.name: Manipulation time
metrics.caveat: A trial receives a time score only if the final cube state is correct; the paper does not state another caveat.

controls.name: Dead reckoning without sensor feedback
controls.detail: The PR2 uses an initial camera-based cube-pose estimate and then executes the finite-state-machine trajectories without further sensor feedback; the sensor-aided condition re-estimates pose before re-grasps.
controls.rules_out: A difference between these conditions supports the contribution of pose re-estimation during manipulation, rather than the finite-state-machine approach alone.

evidence_standards.name: Mean and standard deviation across repeated trials
evidence_standards.detail: For tiers with five consecutive trials, the paper reports average manipulation time and standard deviation. Single-trial tiers have no standard deviation. It specifies no statistical test or numerical threshold for deciding that a difference is real.

datasets.name: RLBench
datasets.eval_protocol: Few-shot challenge v1.0: 10% of the 100 tasks are held out for meta-test and the rest used for meta-training. At test time, provide 1, 5, or 20 demonstrations of each unseen task and report success on new episodes of that task. The paper does not specify a test-episode count.

datasets.name: 10-task simulated robotic manipulation benchmark (CSIRO real-world motion-capture dataset)
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the ten protocol-defined tasks: two kinematic arm tasks and eight object-manipulation tasks. Each real-world task has 20 repeats; each simulated task is also run for 20 repeats, with simulation data recorded at 10 Hz. Simulation uses the task protocol’s scene, starting poses, joint-position sequence, and proportional joint-velocity control. Results are compared with the real-world recordings; object final resting positions and rotations are compared with distributions fitted from the 20 real-world repeats. Tasks are reported in subgroups: Tasks 1–2 and Tasks 3–10. ROS bag data is converted to CSV; the supplied summary CSV gives mean arm, force/torque, joint-torque, and finger-position data and retains object poses across repeats.

baselines.name: PyBullet (Bullet 3)
baselines.fair_comparison: Run on the same ten task protocols, robot description and task scenes, with joint-velocity proportional control at 10 Hz and 20 repeats. Most settings were left at simulator defaults; the reported setup changes the robot-base position and object weights, and changes V-Rep finger-joint settings as specified.

baselines.name: V-Rep (Bullet 2.78)
baselines.fair_comparison: Run on the same ten task protocols, robot description and task scenes, with joint-velocity proportional control at 10 Hz and 20 repeats. Most settings were left at simulator defaults; the reported setup changes the robot-base position and object weights, and changes V-Rep finger-joint settings as specified.

baselines.name: V-Rep (Bullet 2.83)
baselines.fair_comparison: Run on the same ten task protocols, robot description and task scenes, with joint-velocity proportional control at 10 Hz and 20 repeats. Most settings were left at simulator defaults; the reported setup changes the robot-base position and object weights, and changes V-Rep finger-joint settings as specified.

baselines.name: V-Rep (Newton)
baselines.fair_comparison: Run on the same ten task protocols, robot description and task scenes, with joint-velocity proportional control at 10 Hz and 20 repeats. Most settings were left at simulator defaults; the reported setup changes the robot-base position and object weights, and changes V-Rep finger-joint settings as specified.

baselines.name: V-Rep (ODE)
baselines.fair_comparison: Run on the same ten task protocols, robot description and task scenes, with joint-velocity proportional control at 10 Hz and 20 repeats. Most settings were left at simulator defaults; the reported setup changes the robot-base position and object weights, and changes V-Rep finger-joint settings as specified.

baselines.name: V-Rep (Vortex)
baselines.fair_comparison: Run on the same ten task protocols, robot description and task scenes, with joint-velocity proportional control at 10 Hz and 20 repeats. Most settings were left at simulator defaults; the reported setup changes the robot-base position and object weights, and changes V-Rep finger-joint settings as specified.

metrics.name: Euclidean distance error
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that Euclidean and rotation errors can show only a small window of deviation; it presents pose error as a more informative way to distinguish translation and rotation discrepancies.

metrics.name: Inner product of unit quaternion rotation error
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that Euclidean and rotation errors can show only a small window of deviation; it presents pose error as a more informative way to distinguish translation and rotation discrepancies.

metrics.name: End-effector velocity: maximum, average, and error
Manipulable-object velocity: maximum and average over moving time
metrics.caveat: Velocity error over time cannot be calculated for manipulable objects, so the paper reports their maximum and average velocity instead.

metrics.name: Motor torque: minimum, maximum, and error
Object final translation distribution comparison (Mahalanobis distance)
metrics.caveat: The paper says averaging object trajectories is not valid when objects do not share the same end pose, and that their trajectories cannot be directly compared; it instead compares final resting poses with the dataset distribution.

metrics.name: Object final rotation distribution comparison (Mahalanobis distance)
metrics.caveat: The paper says averaging object trajectories is not valid when objects do not share the same end pose, and that their trajectories cannot be directly compared; it instead compares final resting poses with the dataset distribution.

metrics.name: Mean subgroup error across tasks
metrics.caveat: The paper reports this subgroup summary for comparison while making the additional metrics available because errors alone do not provide the same depth of insight.

evidence_standards.name: 20 repeated runs per task
evidence_standards.detail: The dataset repeats each physical task 20 times, and the benchmark requires 20 simulation repeats. The paper uses these repeats to characterize final object-pose distributions. It specifies no statistical significance test, confidence interval, or numerical margin for deciding that two results differ.

datasets.name: MetaWorld
datasets.eval_protocol: Five tasks: ring onto peg, block pick-and-place between bins, button pushing, drawer opening, and hammering a nail. Use 5, 10, or 25 demonstrations; evaluate across multiple views and target-object positions. Report the best success rate during 20,000 behavior-cloning training steps, with online evaluation every 1,000 steps; average over 3 seeds, views, demonstration sizes, and object positions.

datasets.name: Franka Kitchen
datasets.eval_protocol: Five tasks: opening the right door, opening the left door, turning on the light, turning the stove knob, and opening the microwave. Use 5, 10, or 25 demonstrations; evaluate across multiple views and desk positions. Report the best success rate during 20,000 behavior-cloning training steps, with online evaluation every 1,000 steps; average over 3 seeds, views, demonstration sizes, and task variations.

datasets.name: Adroit
datasets.eval_protocol: Two tasks: pen reorientation and moving a ball to a specified position. Use 25, 50, or 100 demonstrations; evaluate across multiple views and goal positions. Report the best success rate during 20,000 behavior-cloning training steps, with online evaluation every 1,000 steps; average over 3 seeds, views, demonstration sizes, and goals.

baselines.name: CLIP
baselines.fair_comparison: All visual representations are used in the same downstream evaluation protocol, with the same behavior-cloning setup.

baselines.name: ImageNet supervised (ImNet Supervised)
baselines.fair_comparison: All visual representations are used in the same downstream evaluation protocol, with the same behavior-cloning setup.

baselines.name: MoCo (345) (PVR)
baselines.fair_comparison: All visual representations are used in the same downstream evaluation protocol, with the same behavior-cloning setup. The paper notes its MoCo setup differs from Parisi et al. in details such as proprioception features and frame stacking, so numerical results are not directly comparable across papers.

baselines.name: Training from scratch
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared in the same downstream evaluation protocol as the pretrained representations.

baselines.name: MoCo-Ego4D
baselines.fair_comparison: Trained on the exact same Ego4D frames as R3M, with the same compute; evaluated on Franka Kitchen and Adroit.

baselines.name: MVP
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on Franka Kitchen and Adroit; the paper describes MVP as using the same or more data and compute as R3M.

controls.name: R3M(-Aug)
controls.detail: R3M trained without crop augmentations.
controls.rules_out: Whether the full model's performance depends on the crop-augmentation component.

controls.name: R3M(-L1)
controls.detail: R3M trained without L1 regularization.
controls.rules_out: Whether the full model's performance depends on its L1 regularization component.

controls.name: R3M(-Lang)
controls.detail: R3M trained without the video-language alignment loss.
controls.rules_out: Whether the full model's performance depends on video-language alignment.

controls.name: MoCo-Ego4D
controls.detail: MoCo trained on the exact same Ego4D frames as R3M, with the same compute.
controls.rules_out: Whether R3M's gains over other representations are explained by using the Ego4D data alone rather than its training objective.

confounds.name: The gains come from the data rather than R3M's training objective
confounds.detail: Because R3M uses diverse human video data, its downstream gains might be explained by the dataset alone rather than by its temporal, language-alignment, and regularization objectives.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare against MoCo trained on the exact same Ego4D frames with the same compute, and against MVP trained on Ego-soup; evaluate these comparisons on Franka Kitchen and Adroit.

evidence_standards.name: Simulation runs and uncertainty
evidence_standards.detail: Run 3 behavior-cloning seeds per representation and task; report success rates with standard error bars. Evaluate online every 1,000 training steps for 20,000 steps and report the best success rate achieved.

evidence_standards.name: Real-world trials
evidence_standards.detail: Report success out of 10 trials for each task and method.

datasets.name: CALVIN
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate 1000 unique instruction chains, each containing up to 5 language instructions across 34 subtasks. After each sequence, reset the robot to a neutral position; advance to the next instruction only when the current subtask succeeds. Run ablations on environment D. Also evaluate the multi-environment split A,B,C,D→D and the zero-shot multi-environment split A,B,C→D. Each environment has 6 hours of teleoperated play data, with language annotations on 1% of the data. Report success percentages by chain length and average completed chain length.

baselines.name: MCIL
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on CALVIN with the paper’s evaluation protocol. The paper uses the same convolutional image encoders as the CALVIN MCIL baseline and applies its image augmentation to all baselines.

baselines.name: MCIL with delta actions
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on CALVIN using relative actions; the paper reports the comparison in its ablation evaluation.

baselines.name: GCBC with delta actions
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on CALVIN using delta actions; further matching details are not stated.

baselines.name: MPNet SBERT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as a replacement text encoder within the paper’s model; further matching details are not stated.

baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as a replacement text encoder within the paper’s model; further matching details are not stated.

baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as a replacement text encoder within the paper’s model; further matching details are not stated.

baselines.name: BERT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as a replacement text encoder within the paper’s model; further matching details are not stated.

baselines.name: CLIP encoders
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as a replacement visual and language encoder within the paper’s model; further matching details are not stated.

metrics.name: Success rate by number of instructions completed in a row

controls.name: No Transformer Encoder
controls.detail: Replace the multimodal Transformer posterior encoder with a bidirectional GRU.

controls.name: No Discrete Latents

datasets.name: Multi-shape block-pushing (PyMunk simulator)

Maximum episode length is 300; report success rate and episodic length. Includes T-, C-, and L-shaped training blocks and zero-shot evaluation on an unseen I-shaped block. For the released behavior-cloning checkpoint, test across 100 randomized scenarios using the simulator and protocol of [6].

datasets.name: Real-world block-pushing tasks (UR5e setup)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate the learned policy on 36 tasks with variations in block shape, friction, weight, and goal pose. Compare ESM and SAC on 9 training tasks; the table reports success out of 3 trials per shape, plus distance and steps for successful pushes.

datasets.name: VLABench
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates VLA models on primitive tasks with seen and unseen object categories, on out-of-domain language and unseen-but-similar tasks, and on composite tasks. For VLA fine-tuning, the paper samples 100 trajectories per task category (1,600 total) for joint primitive-task training; composite tasks are fine-tuned and evaluated separately by task domain. Workflow methods use a single evaluation setting across ability dimensions. VLM non-interactive evaluation uses simulated task examples with two four-view images (annotated and unannotated) and a randomly selected GPT-4-generated instruction; results are reported in a 1-shot setting except GLM-4V-9B, which uses 0-shot. Interactive VLM evaluation uses task progress in simulation. The paper does not specify evaluation episode counts.

baselines.name: Octo
baselines.fair_comparison: Fine-tuned on the VLABench data and evaluated on the same tasks and settings as the other VLAs; the authors use the original code and default hyperparameters and fix training epochs for comparisons across dataset sizes. baselines.name: OpenVLA
baselines.fair_comparison: Fine-tuned on the VLABench data and evaluated on the same tasks and settings as the other VLAs; the authors use the original code and default hyperparameters and fix training epochs for comparisons across dataset sizes. metrics.caveat: The paper says a 0/1 success score is better suited to straightforward skill learning and is limited for nuanced assessment of generalization; it introduces Progress Score alongside it.

metrics.caveat: The paper presents PS as a more graduated alternative to binary task success; it does not state a specific caveat for PS itself.

controls.name: Voxposer without visual perception
controls.detail: The text-based Voxposer setup is given ground-truth labels for object selection, and is compared with Voxposer using GPT-4V for visual perception.
controls.rules_out: The comparison measures the effect of adding a visual-perception module rather than attributing all Voxposer performance to the language-model workflow alone.

controls.name: VLA fine-tuning from scratch
controls.detail: OpenVLA, Octo, and RDT-1B are trained from scratch on the fine-tuning data and compared with their pretrained counterparts on primitive tasks with seen objects.
controls.rules_out: The comparison tests whether the reported fine-tuned performance depends on pretrained initialization.

controls.name: RDT-1B closed-loop control
controls.detail: Compared with the main open-loop, single-trajectory inference setup using 64 trajectory points.
controls.rules_out: The comparison tests whether low task performance is explained by open-loop error accumulation.

controls.name: VLM evaluation without Chain-of-Thought prompting
controls.detail: Compared with Chain-of-Thought prompting for VLMs.
controls.rules_out: The comparison tests whether performance differences in the CoT experiment depend on adding CoT prompting.

confounds.name: Low VLA performance is due to limited fine-tuning data scale
confounds.detail: The poor scores could reflect too few training examples rather than the claimed limitations in VLA generalization or task capability.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors evaluate three VLAs with 100, 500, 1,000, and 2,000 samples on selected primitive tasks. PS improves slightly with more data, but task success remains notably low across all four scales.

confounds.name: RDT-1B failures are caused by open-loop error accumulation
confounds.detail: Execution errors could accumulate because the primary RDT-1B evaluation uses open-loop control, rather than reflecting an inherent model limitation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They evaluate RDT-1B with closed-loop control; it performs only slightly better than open-loop control, which the authors interpret as evidence that model limitations are the primary cause.

confounds.name: Voxposer's spatial-task results reflect missing visual perception
confounds.detail: Weak spatial performance could result from Voxposer lacking visual input, rather than from the workflow's other limitations.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They compare Voxposer without visual perception, which receives ground-truth labels, with a version using GPT-4V. Visual perception improves spatial reasoning but slightly reduces performance in semantic understanding and reasoning.

confounds.name: CoPA failures are explained by segmentation-parameter sensitivity
confounds.detail: Incorrect entity recognition could arise from sensitivity of the SoM segmentation module to its parameters.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors report extensive parameter tuning but say substantial incorrect object-recognition cases persisted.

evidence_standards.name: Repeated workflow evaluations with aggregation
evidence_standards.detail: The paper says each workflow task is evaluated several times and the scores are aggregated, but it does not give the number of repetitions or report a variance measure or statistical test.

evidence_standards.name: VLM prompting setting
evidence_standards.detail: The main VLM comparison is reported under 1-shot prompting; GLM-4V-9B is evaluated 0-shot because it does not support the required multiple-image input. The paper reports no seed count, confidence intervals, or statistical significance test.

datasets.name: OCRTOC 2020 simulation contest
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on 100 contest tasks using both PyBullet and SAPIEN; the better result across the two simulators was used. Object-pose ground truth was used for scoring. Task error is the average across objects of capped 3D Euclidean pose-distance error; overall performance is averaged across tasks.

datasets.name: OCRTOC 2020 real-robot contest
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on five contest tasks. Each contestant was run three times and the best performance was used. Each task was limited to 10 minutes. Task error is the average across objects of capped 3D Euclidean pose-distance error; overall performance is averaged across tasks.

metrics.name: Task and overall error
metrics.caveat: Per-object distance error is capped at an object-size-dependent upper bound so a poorly manipulated object, such as one knocked away, does not dominate the score; task error averages capped errors across objects, and overall error averages across tasks.

evidence_standards.name: Simulation evaluation aggregation
evidence_standards.detail: Solutions were evaluated in both simulators, and the better result was used as the contestant's final performance; no seeds, variance estimates, or statistical tests are reported.

evidence_standards.name: Real-robot evaluation aggregation
evidence_standards.detail: Each contestant was evaluated three times and the best performance was used; rankings were based on error, with execution time breaking ties. No variance estimates or statistical tests are reported.

datasets.name: Machine-Generated (MG): Lift and Can
datasets.eval_protocol: Collected from RL-agent checkpoints, with 300 rollout trajectories per checkpoint. Evaluated on low-dimensional observations; each checkpoint is evaluated with 50 rollouts, and the best success rate over training is averaged across 3 seeds.

datasets.name: Proficient-Human (PH)
datasets.eval_protocol: 200 demonstrations per task from one experienced teleoperator; evaluated on Lift, Can, Square, Transport, and Tool Hang in simulation, using low-dimensional and image observations. Each checkpoint is evaluated with 50 rollouts; the best success rate over training is averaged across 3 seeds.

datasets.name: Multi-Human (MH)
datasets.eval_protocol: 300 demonstrations per task from 6 teleoperators (50 each: 2 better, 2 okay, 2 worse); evaluated on Lift, Can, Square, Transport, and Tool Hang in simulation, using low-dimensional and image observations. Each checkpoint is evaluated with 50 rollouts; the best success rate over training is averaged across 3 seeds.

datasets.name: MH proficiency subsets: Can-Worse/Okay/Better and Square-Worse/Okay/Better
datasets.eval_protocol: Each 100-demo subset corresponds to the two operators in the named proficiency group. Evaluated with the common simulation protocol: 50 rollouts per checkpoint, best success rate over training, averaged across 3 seeds.

datasets.name: MH mixed-proficiency subsets: Can-Worse-Okay, Can-Worse-Better, Can-Okay-Better; Square-Worse-Okay, Square-Worse-Better, Square-Okay-Better
datasets.eval_protocol: Each 200-demo subset combines the named 100-demo proficiency subsets. Evaluated with the common simulation protocol: 50 rollouts per checkpoint, best success rate over training, averaged across 3 seeds.

datasets.name: Can-Paired
datasets.eval_protocol: 200 demonstrations from one operator: one success and one failure for each of 100 task initializations. Evaluated with 50 rollouts per checkpoint; best success rate over training, averaged across 3 seeds.

datasets.name: Reduced-size human datasets (20% and 50% subsets)
datasets.eval_protocol: Formed by sampling trajectories from human datasets; BC-RNN evaluated on low-dimensional and image observations. Uses the simulation evaluation protocol of 50 rollouts per checkpoint, best success rate over training, averaged across 3 seeds.

datasets.name: Lift (Real), Can (Real), Tool Hang (Real)
datasets.eval_protocol: Each dataset contains 200 trajectories from one operator. BC-RNN is evaluated at the final checkpoint over 30 real-world rollouts; no real-world hyperparameter tuning is performed.

datasets.name: DROID

datasets.name: In-house fabric manipulation data
datasets.eval_protocol: 2,662 questions across ten fabric-manipulation dimensions, generally one question per recorded scene and without question augmentation. Questions have four choices; models are evaluated by accuracy. Data for which preprocessing failed is discarded.

datasets.name: Simulated cube reorientation
datasets.eval_protocol: Train with 16,384 agents per GPU; evaluate goal-reaching with a 0.4 rad orientation threshold (training threshold 0.1 rad). No evaluation episode count is specified.

datasets.name: Real-world cube reorientation (Allegro Hand)
datasets.eval_protocol: Run 10 trials per policy and report consecutive target orientations achieved before dropping the cube or remaining stuck for over 80 seconds; repeat trial sets on different days. The target threshold is 0.4 rad. A separate condition holds each target for 10 consecutive frames before refreshing it.

datasets.name: Pose-estimation test set (simulation)

baselines.name: Manual-DR (non-ADR) policy
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with the paper’s ADR policies on the same real-world reorientation task; the paper describes the non-ADR policy as using manually tuned domain-randomization ranges.

baselines.name: OpenAI et al. [1] block-reorientation policies (state, locked-wrist state, and vision)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on block reorientation, but the paper notes that the comparison is not direct: OpenAI used a Shadow Hand, while this paper uses a four-finger Allegro Hand with a locked wrist.

baselines.name: OpenAI et al. [8] ADR policies (L, XL, and XXL; state input)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on block reorientation, but the paper notes differences in hardware and state sensing; the OpenAI policies used PhaseSpace markers, whereas this paper’s policy uses vision.

metrics.name: Consecutive successes
metrics.caveat: A target may be reached briefly because the cube shoots past it or because of pose-estimation noise; the paper also notes that prior work capped successes at 50. It reports a separate 10-frame target-hold condition and gives results capped at 50 for comparison.

metrics.name: Average consecutive successes
metrics.caveat: Results vary between trial sets and days; the paper reports 10 trials per policy, 90% confidence intervals, and results from different days.

metrics.name: Median consecutive successes
metrics.caveat: The paper reports it alongside the average because trial outcomes vary; it also reports results from different days.

metrics.name: Average rotation error
metrics.caveat: The pose estimator can only be precisely evaluated in simulation because the real-world setup does not use a marker-based reference system; reported with a 90% confidence interval.

metrics.name: Average translation error (X, Y, Z)
metrics.caveat: The pose estimator can only be precisely evaluated in simulation because the real-world setup does not use a marker-based reference system; reported per axis with 90% confidence intervals.

metrics.name: Nats per dimension (npd)
metrics.caveat: The paper says it does not directly capture environment difficulty because dimensions are not normalized for difficulty; it is only a rough proxy for the amount of randomization.

controls.name: Manual-DR (non-ADR) policy
controls.detail: A policy trained with manually tuned domain-randomization ranges, evaluated alongside the ADR policy.
controls.rules_out: That the reported advantage is explained by domain randomization alone, rather than the paper’s ADR-based range adjustment.

confounds.name: A counted goal could be a brief overshoot or pose-estimation noise rather than a reliably achieved target orientation
confounds.detail: The paper notes that the cube may shoot past a target, making it hard to tell whether a counted success reflects accurate pose estimation or chance noise.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Run a separate real-world condition that refreshes the target only after the cube stays within the 0.4 rad threshold for 10 consecutive frames; the paper also compares this with simulation frame-hold results.

evidence_standards.name: 10 real-world trials per policy; report mean and 90% confidence interval, plus median
evidence_standards.detail: The paper also collects trial sets on different days to examine inter-day variability. It does not specify a statistical significance test or a threshold for declaring a difference real.

evidence_standards.name: Pose-estimation errors reported with 90% confidence intervals
evidence_standards.detail: Reported on a 50,000-image simulation test set; no statistical test or decision threshold is specified.

baselines.name: Task-specific trained models
baselines.fair_comparison: Trained separately for each object in each task group; the paper uniformly set the test background to green for experimental fairness.

baselines.name: Previous work [7] (needle-threading)
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper notes that the data amount and environment, including lighting, differed, so the results cannot be directly compared.

controls.name: No gaze
controls.detail: Removes visual attention and uses global vision instead of foveated vision; the ablation models have the same number of policy-predictor parameters as DAA.
controls.rules_out: A gain attributable to visual attention rather than merely using the DAA model; lower success supports the importance of visual attention.

controls.name: No dual
controls.detail: Removes dual-action, treating all actions as reactive; the ablation models have the same number of policy-predictor parameters as DAA.
controls.rules_out: A gain attributable to dual-action rather than merely using the DAA model; lower success supports the importance of dual-action.

confounds.name: The gains come from model size rather than the attention or dual-action mechanisms
confounds.detail: A larger policy predictor could explain higher success without the proposed mechanisms being responsible.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The No gaze and No dual ablations have the same number of policy-predictor parameters as DAA, and both achieve lower success rates.

evidence_standards.name: Real-robot trial counts and success rates
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports 7,815 total trials; in the multi-task evaluation, tasks were attempted 9–36 times each. It reports success rates but specifies no seeds, variance estimates, statistical test, or threshold for treating a difference as real.

datasets.name: RLBench
datasets.eval_protocol: Experiments use simulation data in CoppeliaSim; language annotations are generated from manually designed templates and keyframes are extracted by monitoring robot state and task-related events. The paper reports quantitative results on its Kitchen and Living Room benchmarks; it does not give a separate RLBench split or trial count.

datasets.name: Kitchen
datasets.eval_protocol: 10 manipulation skills; each skill has 20 training episodes and 25 test episodes, with variations in attributes such as color, size, count, placement, and object category (69 distinct variations total). Evaluates settings 5-5 and 5-1; reports success scores by skill and for base, novel, and all skills, plus average performance and forgetting rate.

datasets.name: Living Room
datasets.eval_protocol: 12 manipulation skills; each skill has 20 training episodes and 25 test episodes, with variations in attributes such as color, size, count, placement, and object category (69 distinct variations total). Evaluates settings 6-3 and 6-2; reports success scores by skill and for base, novel, and all skills, plus average performance and forgetting rate.

baselines.fair_comparison: Used as a joint-training upper bound, training all manipulation skills in one stage. The paper applies the same RT-1 base behavior-cloning agent and reports shared optimizer settings; it does not describe this as a sequential-learning-matched comparison.

baselines.name: GNFactor
baselines.fair_comparison: Used as a joint-training upper bound, training all manipulation skills in one stage. The paper applies the same RT-1 base behavior-cloning agent and reports shared optimizer settings; it does not describe this as a sequential-learning-matched comparison.

baselines.fair_comparison: Uses RT-1 as the base agent; comparison methods use the reported common LAMB optimizer, initial learning rate of 5.0×10^-4, and batch size of 2. The paper states that four episodes of each old skill are stored for all methods.

metrics.name: Success score (%)
metrics.caveat: A final success score alone does not describe performance over the whole continual-learning process; the paper also reports average performance and forgetting rate.

metrics.name: Base success score
metrics.caveat: Measures the final score for skills learned in the base task; the paper also reports novel-skill and all-skill scores.

metrics.name: Novel success score
metrics.caveat: Measures the final score for skills learned in continual tasks; the paper also reports base-skill and all-skill scores.

metrics.name: All success score
metrics.caveat: Measures the final mean success score across all learned skills; the paper also reports average performance and forgetting rate over the learning process.

metrics.name: Avg. (G)
metrics.caveat: Averages the all-skill success score across the continual-learning tasks; the paper also reports the final scores and forgetting rate.

metrics.name: For. (F)
metrics.caveat: Measures skill-wise forgetting as the average, across skills, of the maximum earlier score minus the final score; the paper also reports success scores and Avg.

controls.name: Base (no SSR, SEP, or SRD)
controls.detail: Ablation condition without the proposed modules.
controls.rules_out: Provides a no-module reference for the module ablations; differences do not by themselves isolate any one module.

controls.name: Base+SSR
controls.detail: Ablation condition with SSR but without SEP and SRD.
controls.rules_out: Comparisons with the base condition measure the combined effect of adding SSR in that ablation setup.

controls.name: Base+SSR+SEP (without SRD)
controls.detail: Ablation condition with SSR and SEP, but without SRD.
controls.rules_out: Comparison with the full method tests the contribution of SRD when SSR and SEP are present.

controls.name: Base+SSR+SRD (without SEP)
controls.detail: Ablation condition with SSR and SRD, but without SEP.
controls.rules_out: Comparison with the full method tests the contribution of SEP when SSR and SRD are present.

controls.name: Base (NeRF-only rendering)
controls.detail: SSR ablation using NeRF-only rendering without the external semantic model.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the full SSR result depends on semantic supervision beyond NeRF rendering alone.

controls.name: Base+DINO
controls.detail: SSR ablation replacing Stable Diffusion with DINO.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the result is specific to the Stable Diffusion semantic supervision rather than another vision model.

controls.name: Base+CLIP
controls.detail: SSR ablation replacing Stable Diffusion with CLIP.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the result is specific to the Stable Diffusion semantic supervision rather than another vision-language model.

confounds.name: The result may depend on which external model supplies SSR semantic features
confounds.detail: Performance gains could reflect the choice of semantic feature provider rather than the proposed SSR approach more generally.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Ablates SSR supervision using NeRF-only rendering and substitutions with DINO and CLIP, and compares these with the Stable Diffusion version.

confounds.name: Task order may account for the reported continual-learning performance
confounds.detail: A favorable order of skills could produce the headline scores without the method being robust to skill sequence.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluates three randomized task orders and reports that performance fluctuations are within about 2%.

confounds.name: Memory-buffer size may account for differences in forgetting
confounds.detail: More stored old-skill episodes can reduce forgetting independently of the proposed mechanisms.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Uses four old-skill episodes in the method comparisons and separately reports results with buffer sizes 2, 4, and 6.

evidence_standards.name: Three randomized task orders
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports results across three task orders and describes fluctuations as minor, within about 2%; it reports no seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical tests.

datasets.name: VLMbench
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated in seen and unseen settings on test configurations drawn from a pre-collected test dataset, separately by task variation. The paper does not state the number of episodes. It reports success rate as the number of satisfied success conditions divided by the number of tests, and averages success rates across variations for each task category. Success is determined mainly by object or joint detectors. Before testing, tasks are divided into sub-goal sequences using AMSolver ground-truth waypoints; gripper open/close state is provided; a pre-generated grasp pose replaces the estimate when distance is under 5 cm and rotation difference is under 10 degrees; pre-grasp and post-grasp offsets of 8 cm are applied.

baselines.name: Language-Only agent
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the same model architecture as 6D-CLIPort; visual inputs are all zeros, while the CLIP transformer encodes language.

baselines.name: Vision-Only agent
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the same model architecture and RGB-D inputs as 6D-CLIPort; its language input contains only a step-indication prompt, without the high-level instruction.

controls.name: Language-Only agent
controls.detail: A modality ablation with visual inputs set to zero; language encoding is retained.
controls.rules_out: If it performs worse than 6D-CLIPort, language input alone is not sufficient to explain the full model's performance.

controls.name: Vision-Only agent
controls.detail: A modality ablation that retains RGB-D input but removes the high-level language instruction, retaining only the step prompt.
controls.rules_out: If it performs worse than 6D-CLIPort, visual input alone is not sufficient to explain the full model's performance.

controls.name: 6D-CLIPort (GT Ori)
controls.detail: Provides ground-truth orientation while estimating position.
controls.rules_out: Shows how performance changes when orientation estimation is removed as a source of error.

controls.name: 6D-CLIPort (GT Pos)
controls.detail: Provides ground-truth x/y/z positions while estimating orientation.
controls.rules_out: Shows how performance changes when position estimation is removed as a source of error.

confounds.name: Some Vision-Only successes may come from randomly grasping objects rather than language-guided reasoning
confounds.detail: The paper notes that Vision-Only can succeed in a few lower-variance tasks by randomly grasping an object and manipulating it.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare Vision-Only with 6D-CLIPort; the paper reports substantially lower Vision-Only success and failures on tasks with stricter pose constraints.

confounds.name: Some Language-Only drawer successes may come from collisions rather than correctly grounded manipulation
confounds.detail: The paper notes that language can reveal drawer level and action direction, allowing the Language-Only agent to close drawers by collisions.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare Language-Only with 6D-CLIPort; the paper reports near-zero Language-Only success overall, including low drawer success.

datasets.name: Bimanual Robotic Manipulation of Semi-Deformable Objects benchmark
datasets.eval_protocol: Two tasks: watchmaking, evaluated with the big and small watch scales, and rubber-band manipulation. Each task uses 3 different initial object orientations and 5 repetitions per orientation; watchmaking is repeated for each scale. Results are reported per sub-task. Global scores include success rate (successful trials divided by all trials) and normalized average completion time, with time capped at 60 s. The paper specifies no train/test split or preprocessing.

baselines.name: Adaptive Control (AC) baseline
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the centralized QP control scheme and predefined end-effector waypoints. The paper compares the same algorithm using motion-capture poses and the benchmark computer-vision poses.

baselines.name: Offline Learning baseline #1 (OFL#1)
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the centralized QP control scheme and assumes a plan is given; learns pose corrections from 200 samples pairing computer-vision estimates with motion-capture estimates.

baselines.name: Offline Learning baseline #2 (OFL#2)
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the centralized QP control scheme and pose-correction models; extracts waypoints from one teleoperated demonstration using graph-based kernel PCA.

metrics.name: Normalized number of offline real-world samples (A1)

controls.name: AC baseline with motion-capture tracking
controls.detail: Runs the same AC algorithm as the computer-vision condition, but with motion-capture pose measurements reported as accurate to less than 1 mm.
controls.rules_out: A poor result with computer vision alone being attributable simply to the predefined plan or controller being unable to perform the task; the comparison tests performance with accurate versus noisy tracking.

confounds.name: Poor performance is due to noisy computer-vision tracking rather than the controller's ability to execute the task
confounds.detail: The AC baseline fails with benchmark computer vision, so the failure could reflect tracking noise rather than inability to execute its plan under accurate state estimates.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Run the same AC algorithm with motion-capture poses and compare it with the computer-vision condition; the paper reports good performance with motion capture and failure every time with computer vision.

evidence_standards.name: Repeated trials across initial orientations
evidence_standards.detail: The protocol specifies 5 repetitions for each of 3 initial orientations; watchmaking is evaluated at both scales. The paper specifies no statistical test, variance interval, or threshold for treating a difference as real.

datasets.name: LIBERO
datasets.eval_protocol: Probe evaluated separately on Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long suites; instructions replaced by learned per-task embeddings. Probe trained and tuned per suite, with the best of several suite-evaluated checkpoints reported. For sample-overfitting analysis, the initial-state file was redrawn from the same generator and each policy ran 10,000 rollouts; significance analysis pools three suites.

For distribution-overfitting analysis, the commonly used ABC→D protocol evaluates five-task language-conditioned chains by average tasks completed (ATC); block poses were resampled within the training range with everything else held fixed. For sample-overfitting analysis, two fresh sequence manifests were drawn from the official generator.

datasets.name: SimplerEnv
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on the WidowX stack task. The overfitting check reverses the instruction, puts the target block on a support block, and resamples block positions and initial arm pose; each change is reported against a matched local rerun of the official protocol. For data-source dependence, the paper reports 92/96 for X-VLA and 91/96 for the separately trained small policies.
