metrics.name: Success rate
metrics.caveat: An aggregate success rate alone generally does not retain the task-level and sample-level information needed to test whether a reported gap is statistically significant; the paper derives significance bounds from aggregate scores and uses paired outcomes when available.

metrics.name: Average tasks completed (ATC)
metrics.caveat: As an aggregate score, ATC alone does not establish whether a reported gap is statistically significant; the paper uses task- and sample-level outcomes to assess significance where available.

metrics.name: Provably significant share of SOTA claims
metrics.caveat: Aggregate scores often cannot determine significance: the paper distinguishes gains that cannot possibly be significant, gains guaranteed significant, and inconclusive gains using bounds; it reports these shares at a 5% significance level.

controls.name: Official fixed-pose CALVIN ABC→D condition
controls.detail: Compared with block poses resampled within the training range while everything else is held fixed.
controls.rules_out: A difference is attributable to reliance on the fixed evaluation poses rather than other changes to the evaluation setup.

controls.name: Official WidowX stack condition with matched local calibration
controls.detail: The official SimplerEnv stack protocol is rerun as a matched local calibration alongside each of the three changed conditions.
controls.rules_out: Provides the reference for measuring the effect of each in-distribution input change.

controls.name: Original LIBERO initial-state sample with matched local calibration
controls.detail: Redrawn initial states from the same generator are compared against a matched local calibration.
controls.rules_out: Separates movement associated with the redrawn sample from the local calibration reference.

controls.name: Original CALVIN sequence manifests with matched local calibration
controls.detail: Two fresh manifests from the official generator are compared with matched local calibrations.
controls.rules_out: Provides a reference for estimating movement due to redrawing the fixed evaluation sample.

confounds.name: CALVIN pose-resampling drops reflect out-of-distribution inputs rather than overfitting to fixed poses
confounds.detail: A performance drop could result from weak generalization to poses outside the policy's training distribution.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Resample block poses from the same training range and hold everything else fixed.

confounds.name: SimplerEnv input-change drops reflect out-of-distribution inputs rather than overfitting
confounds.detail: Changes to instructions, support surfaces, block positions, or initial arm pose could otherwise make evaluation harder by leaving the training distribution.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper checks that all three changes appear in the training set about as often as the official conditions.

confounds.name: Sample-redraw score movements reflect rollout noise rather than sample overfitting
confounds.detail: Closed-loop rollouts are not bitwise deterministic, so observed movement could be noise and its sign uncertain.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Use matched local calibrations; report that LIBERO movements are under one percentage point and CALVIN movements are at most 0.11 ATC, no larger than the calibration noise and far below the CALVIN pose-resampling drops.

confounds.name: A high SimplerEnv score reflects training-data proximity rather than general capability
confounds.detail: Because training data is unrestricted, a policy can train on demonstrations collected right beside the simulated test instead of generalizing from distant real-world data.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper demonstrates the alternative directly: separately trained 22M policies using 120 scripted expert demonstrations recorded beside the test reach 94.8% (91/96), close to X-VLA's reported 95.8% (92/96).

confounds.name: A reported aggregate-score gain is sampling variation rather than a real improvement
confounds.detail: Top-line averages omit the paired task- and sample-level outcomes needed to determine the variance of the gap.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Use a one-sided paired Wald test with task-stratified variance when paired outcomes are available; for aggregate scores, derive feasibility and guarantee bounds and classify intermediate cases as inconclusive.

evidence_standards.name: One-sided paired Wald test at a 5% significance level
evidence_standards.detail: For policies evaluated on the same instances, test improvement with a task-stratified variance estimator. Aggregate-score bounds identify gains that cannot be significant and gains that must be significant; gains between those bounds are inconclusive.

evidence_standards.name: Stratified two-sample Wald test for iid, unpaired evaluations
evidence_standards.detail: The paper identifies this as the natural reference procedure when policies use separate iid samples; because paired outcome data are unavailable, it applies the paired envelopes as conservative, non-sharp top-line cutoffs.

datasets.name: SIMPLER — Google Robot evaluation setup
datasets.eval_protocol: Paired real-world and simulated evaluations of Google Robot tasks, including Pick Coke Can, Move Near, and drawer tasks. The paper reports approximately 1,500 evaluation episodes across its experiments overall; task-specific trial counts are referred to in the supplementary material but are not given in the supplied text. Google Robot simulated results are averaged across four robot-arm/gripper color versions.

metrics.name: Success rate
metrics.caveat: Average performance does not by itself show sensitivity to distribution shifts; the paper also reports success-rate changes under shifts relative to the base environment.

metrics.name: Pearson correlation coefficient (Pearson r)
metrics.caveat: Measures linear consistency, so it can penalize a simulator that preserves policy rankings without a linear relationship; it can also change sharply when real-world performances are close and small differences may be evaluation noise. The paper reports MMRV alongside it.

metrics.name: Validation action MSE
metrics.caveat: The paper finds it is a poor proxy for real-world policy performance and reports MMRV and Pearson r for evaluation-protocol comparisons.

metrics.name: Control loss
metrics.caveat: Measures trajectory tracking using the system-identification loss combining translation and rotation errors; no caveat is stated.

metrics.name: Change in success rate under a distribution shift (ΔSuccess)

controls.name: Perturbed stiffness and damping parameters
controls.detail: The Google Robot evaluation is repeated with perturbed controller parameters instead of the parameters selected by system identification.
controls.rules_out: That the improved real-to-sim correlation is unrelated to using accurately identified control parameters.

controls.name: Visual-matching ablation conditions
controls.detail: The drawer-task comparison includes no visual matching, texture matching without green-screening, green-screening alone, green-screening with drawer matching only, and green-screening with both drawer and robot matching.
controls.rules_out: That the visual-matching result is explained by only one component; the reported best correlation uses green-screening together with tuned foreground assets.

controls.name: Variant Aggregation
controls.detail: Visual scene aspects are heavily randomized into environment variants and evaluation results are aggregated, as an alternative to the main Visual Matching setup.
controls.rules_out: That the correlation depends merely on evaluating across multiple visual variants rather than on matching simulation visuals to the real environment.

controls.name: Perturbed physical properties
controls.detail: For Pick Coke Can, the paper varies can density/mass and gripper-finger static friction; for drawer tasks, it varies cabinet joint friction.
controls.rules_out: That the reported evaluation correlation requires precise modeling of these physical properties.

controls.name: Alternative physics simulator (Isaac Sim)
controls.detail: The Google Robot evaluation is reproduced in Isaac Sim as well as the default SAPIEN setup.
controls.rules_out: That the reported correlation is specific to the SAPIEN physics simulator.

controls.name: Base environment without a distribution shift
controls.detail: Success under each tested distribution shift is compared with success in the base environment; the shift result averages two variations per axis.
controls.rules_out: That the measured shift effect is simply the policy's base-task performance rather than a change associated with the tested shift.

confounds.name: Control dynamics mismatch between simulation and reality
confounds.detail: A real-to-sim performance relationship could be poor or misleading because the same actions produce different robot trajectories in simulation and on the real robot.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper system-identifies controller parameters using offline demonstration trajectories, measures open-loop trajectory tracking with translation and rotation losses, and compares real-to-sim MMRV under perturbed versus identified parameters.

confounds.name: Visual differences between simulation and reality
confounds.detail: A policy’s apparent simulated performance or ranking could reflect sensitivity to visual distribution shift rather than its real-world performance.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper compares visual-matching components and Variant Aggregation, measures paired real/sim performance, and tests whether simulated success-rate changes under background, lighting, distractor, table-texture, and camera-pose shifts match real-world changes.

confounds.name: Simplified object and robot physical properties
confounds.detail: Correlation might depend on physical properties such as object mass, gripper friction, or articulated-joint friction being modeled precisely, despite the paper’s use of simplified properties.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper varies can mass/density and gripper friction for Pick Coke Can and cabinet joint friction for drawer tasks, then reports MMRV and Pearson correlation.

confounds.name: Choice of physics simulator
confounds.detail: The results might be an artifact of the default SAPIEN simulator rather than a property of the evaluation approach.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reproduces Google Robot evaluations in Isaac Sim and reports real-to-sim performance correlations there.

confounds.name: Robot arm texture changes during real rollouts
confounds.detail: A single simulated arm color could make results depend on a visual mismatch that changes over the course of real robot videos.
confounds.ruled_out_by: For Google Robot simulated evaluations, the paper averages results over four robot arm and gripper color versions.

confounds.name: Small, noisy real-world performance differences
confounds.detail: Pearson correlation can change substantially when policies have similar real-world performance, so minor evaluation noise could appear to indicate a changed relationship.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports MMRV alongside Pearson r; MMRV weights rank violations by the real-world performance margin.

evidence_standards.name: Three random seeds for Octo simulated evaluations
evidence_standards.detail: Octo simulated success rates are averaged across three random seeds to produce a lower-variance estimate.

evidence_standards.name: Four robot arm/gripper color versions for Google Robot simulation
evidence_standards.detail: Google Robot simulated evaluation results are averaged across four arm and gripper color versions; this step is skipped for WidowX.

evidence_standards.name: Two variations per distribution-shift axis
evidence_standards.detail: The reported ΔSuccess for a shift averages the success-rate differences for two variations against the base environment.

metrics.name: L2 distance between clean and attacked encoded feature vectors

controls.name: Clean, unperturbed observations
controls.detail: Runs the policy on clean images as a reference condition.
controls.rules_out: Whether the task performance change is relative to the policy’s unperturbed performance.

controls.name: Random Gaussian noise attack
controls.detail: Adds random Gaussian noise to observation images as a baseline attack condition.
controls.rules_out: Whether performance degradation is caused merely by adding random image noise rather than the optimized adversarial perturbation.

controls.name: Random noise patch
controls.detail: Evaluates a patch made of random noise alongside the optimized adversarial patch.
controls.rules_out: Whether patch-related performance degradation is explained merely by putting a noisy patch in the scene.

confounds.name: Any image disturbance, rather than an optimized adversarial perturbation, causes the performance drop
confounds.detail: The reported success-rate reduction could arise from ordinary random perturbations rather than the claimed adversarial attack.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compares against random Gaussian noise attacks and random noise patches; reports that optimized attacks degrade performance more than these random-noise conditions.

evidence_standards.name: 50 rollouts per attack condition
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports average task score or success rate across 50 rollouts; for the end-to-end loss comparison it specifies 50 randomly initialized environments. It does not state a variance estimate, statistical test, or threshold for treating differences as real.

datasets.name: LEMMA
datasets.eval_protocol: Per task type, 700 sessions for training, 40 for validation, and 60 for testing; test performance is evaluated with high-level and human instructions. Tasks are evaluated for 10 runs, with success defined as meeting the goal conditions by the end of the episode within a 100-second limit. Visual input is reconstructed as a top-down orthographic RGB-D scene from the RGB-D images, camera parameters, and fused point cloud.

controls.name: Ground-truth task allocation (GTA)
controls.detail: Replace the predicted robot task allocations with ground-truth allocations while preserving the predicted action primitives and objects.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether errors in task allocation account for performance loss, apart from errors in predicted primitives and objects.

confounds.name: Task-allocation errors rather than primitive or object-prediction errors explain failures
confounds.detail: The system may fail because it assigns a sub-task to the wrong robot, rather than because it predicts the wrong action primitive or object.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare with GTA, which supplies ground-truth allocations while retaining predicted primitives and objects; performance improves with this intervention.

evidence_standards.name: 10 evaluation runs; mean and standard deviation
evidence_standards.detail: The authors evaluate all tasks for 10 runs because Isaac Sim physics and rendering are nondeterministic, and report means and standard deviations.

datasets.name: Continuous Object-in-Bowl
datasets.eval_protocol: Real-world continuous task: repeatedly place a plush toy in a bowl, dump it, and repeat for 40 seconds. Randomly selected from 3 bowls and 5 toys, with positions within a 45 cm × 60 cm area. 45 evaluation rollouts across 9 bowl-toy-position combinations. Score one point for each toy placement or bowl emptying. An unseen-scene evaluation is also reported; its rollout count is not stated.

datasets.name: Laundry
datasets.eval_protocol: Real-world task: fold a randomly posed t-shirt within a 90 cm × 60 cm area and ±30° rotation range by folding the right sleeve, left sleeve, and shirt in half. 40 evaluation rollouts across 8 shirt-position combinations. Award points for each stage; SR is the percentage of runs in which all stages succeed. An unseen-shirt-color evaluation is also reported; its rollout count is not stated.

datasets.name: Groceries
datasets.eval_protocol: Real-world task: open a grocery bag by grasping its handle, then place 3 chip packs inside. 50 evaluations across 10 bag positions. Award points for grasping the handle and for each pack placed. Report SR as the percentage of runs with all 3 packs placed and Open Bag as the percentage in which the handle was grasped.

baselines.name: Mimicplay
baselines.fair_comparison: Implemented with the same Transformer backbone as EgoMimic; goal conditioning was removed because EgoMimic is designed for single-task policies. In the unseen-scene comparison, Mimicplay had access to the same information.

metrics.name: Pts (task points)
metrics.caveat: Points count successful task stages or events; for Laundry and Groceries, the paper also reports SR, which requires completion of all specified stages.

metrics.name: SR (success rate)
metrics.caveat: For Laundry, SR requires all folding stages to succeed; for Groceries, it requires all 3 packs to be placed. Groceries also reports Open Bag for the difficult handle-grasping stage.

metrics.name: Open Bag
metrics.caveat: Reports the handle-grasp rate alongside Groceries SR, which requires all 3 packs to be placed.

controls.name: EgoMimic (0% Human) / EgoMimic w/o Hand Data
controls.detail: Runs the EgoMimic architecture without human hand data; the paper compares it with EgoMimic on the tasks and reports an Object-in-Bowl ablation.
controls.rules_out: A gain attributable only to EgoMimic’s architectural changes rather than leveraging human data.

controls.name: EgoMimic w/o Action Norm
controls.detail: Ablates the per-embodiment action normalization; evaluated on Object-in-Bowl.
controls.rules_out: That the Object-in-Bowl improvement is unaffected by the action-normalization mechanism.

controls.name: EgoMimic w/o Line
controls.detail: Removes the red line overlay while retaining masking; evaluated on Object-in-Bowl.
controls.rules_out: That the red line overlay contributes nothing to the reported performance.

controls.name: EgoMimic w/o Line and Mask
controls.detail: Removes both the red line overlay and masking; evaluated on Object-in-Bowl.
controls.rules_out: That the visual alignment techniques contribute nothing to the reported performance.

confounds.name: Improvement comes from architectural changes rather than human data
confounds.detail: EgoMimic changes the ACT architecture, including simultaneous joint- and pose-action prediction, so gains could occur without human demonstrations.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare EgoMimic with EgoMimic (0% Human), which retains the architecture but omits human data; the paper reports the human-data version performs better.

confounds.name: Unseen-scene performance comes from access to human data alone, rather than unified joint hand-robot learning
confounds.detail: A method using the same information from the new scene could potentially generalize just as well without EgoMimic’s unified architecture.
confounds.ruled_out_by: On the unseen-scene Object-in-Bowl evaluation, compare EgoMimic’s 63 points with Mimicplay’s 4 points; the paper says Mimicplay had access to the same information.

confounds.name: Some scaling gain is due to architecture, not the additional human data
confounds.detail: EgoMimic already outperforms ACT at the same 2-hour robot-data amount, so the comparison of 2 hours robot plus 1 hour human against 3 hours robot could partly reflect architecture.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper acknowledges this attribution and reports that EgoMimic at 2 hours of robot data outperforms ACT at 2 hours; it does not isolate the architectural contribution from the human-data contribution in the 3-hour comparison.

evidence_standards.name: Policy rollout setting
evidence_standards.detail: Inference runs at 1 Hz and robot control at 25 Hz; the policy predicts a 4-second action horizon and executes the first second in receding-horizon style.

datasets.name: OpenAI Gym locomotion benchmarks: Hopper-v2, Walker2D-v2, HalfCheetah-v2
datasets.eval_protocol: Pre-train with the full medium-level D4RL datasets, state input, and action chunk size Ta=4; fine-tune with the original dense reward setup. Results are averaged over five seeds.

datasets.name: D4RL Franka-Kitchen: Kitchen-Complete-v0, Kitchen-Partial-v0, Kitchen-Mixed-v0
datasets.eval_protocol: Use state input and Ta=4 for DPPO; fine-tune with the original sparse reward setup. Results are averaged over three seeds.

datasets.name: Robomimic: Lift, Can, Square, Transport
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate with state and pixel inputs. Pre-train state policies with 300 demonstrations and pixel policies with 100; use Multi-Human data mostly and Proficient-Human data in some experiments. Ta=4 for Lift, Can, and Square, and Ta=8 for Transport. Fine-tune with sparse reward equal to 1 upon task completion. Results are averaged over three seeds.

datasets.name: Furniture-Bench: One-leg, Lamp, Round-table
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate simulated tasks at Low and Med initial-state randomness. Pre-train with 50 simulated human demonstrations and Ta=8; fine-tune with sparse reward indicating task-stage completion. Results are averaged over three seeds. One-leg is also evaluated zero-shot on hardware over 20 trials, with policies running at 10 Hz.

datasets.name: D3IL Avoid
datasets.eval_protocol: Use demonstration subsets M1, M2, and M3, each with two modes. Pre-train MLP-based Diffusion, Gaussian, and GMM policies; fine-tune with sparse reward for reaching the goal line from the topmost mode. Compare sampled exploration trajectories at the first fine-tuning iteration; the stability experiment is averaged over five seeds.

baselines.fair_comparison: Fine-tuned with the PPO objective in the policy-parameterization comparisons; diffusion and non-diffusion baselines use the same Ta unless noted.

baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with DPPO on the same simulated Furniture-Bench tasks and randomness settings; results are averaged over three seeds.

baselines.fair_comparison: Fine-tuned with an auxiliary behavior-cloning loss to encourage staying close to the base policy; compared on the One-leg sim-to-real evaluation.

controls.name: Value estimator that also depends on the denoised action
controls.detail: Ablation against the DPPO value estimator that depends only on environment state.
controls.rules_out: A performance difference supports the paper's claim that omitting the denoised action from the value estimator is important for challenging-task performance.

controls.name: Alternative denoising-noise clipping levels
controls.detail: Ablations vary the minimum exploration noise used when sampling actions.
controls.rules_out: Differences test whether DPPO's exploration results depend on the chosen noise clipping level rather than clipping being incidental.

controls.name: Fine-tune fewer than all denoising steps
controls.detail: Ablations compare fine-tuning a subset of denoising steps with fine-tuning all K steps.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the reported performance depends on updating the full denoising chain.

controls.name: Pre-trained-only policy
controls.detail: The One-leg hardware evaluation reports results for policies after pre-training and after DPPO fine-tuning.
controls.rules_out: A difference shows whether the hardware result is already present in the pre-trained policy or follows fine-tuning.

confounds.name: DPPO's advantage could be due to Gaussian or GMM policies failing to represent the demonstration modes
confounds.detail: If the alternatives cannot fit the expert distribution, their fine-tuning performance would be a weak comparison rather than evidence for DPPO's exploration mechanism.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors use the D3IL Avoid environment with simple two-mode demonstration subsets M1, M2, and M3, chosen so Gaussian and GMM policies can fit the data reasonably well, then compare pre-trained policies and their sampled exploration trajectories.

confounds.name: On-manifold exploration may hinder tasks that require aggressive, unstructured exploration
confounds.detail: DPPO could underperform because its structured exploration stays near the pre-training data manifold when successful behavior requires leaving it.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper tests from-scratch exploration and reports no substantial DPPO advantage or disadvantage there; it also reports that DPPO slightly underperforms the Gaussian baseline on Lamp with Low randomness. The authors present this as a limitation, so the concern is not ruled out generally.

confounds.name: The sim-to-real gap for Gaussian policies could be caused by drifting too far from the base policy during fine-tuning
confounds.detail: If fine-tuning drift causes the Gaussian policy's volatile hardware behavior, its failure would not by itself show an advantage specific to DPPO.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors also fine-tune Gaussian with an auxiliary behavior-cloning loss to keep it close to the base policy; it reaches 50% hardware success, below DPPO's 80%.

evidence_standards.name: Five-seed averages
evidence_standards.detail: Gym results are averaged over five seeds; the Avoid training-stability experiment is also averaged over five seeds. The paper does not state a significance test or a numerical margin for calling differences real.

evidence_standards.name: Three-seed averages
evidence_standards.detail: Robomimic, Franka-Kitchen, policy-parameterization, and simulated Furniture-Bench results are reported as averages over three seeds. The paper does not state a significance test or a numerical margin for calling differences real.

evidence_standards.name: Twenty hardware trials
evidence_standards.detail: Zero-shot One-leg sim-to-real success is evaluated over 20 trials; policies run at 10 Hz.
